entries.title: Kitesurf is now open source
entries.summary: Kitesurf, our experimental browser engine for AI agents, is now open source. Inspect the code, run it locally, or deploy your own instance on Cloudflare Workers.
entries.content:
We introduced Kitesurf, our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to.

That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers.

A browser built for agents

Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer.

Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network.

Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation.

What is inside the repository?

Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly:

  • Blitz provides HTML parsing, the DOM, layout, and painting.
  • Stylo provides CSS parsing, cascading, and computed styles.
  • Boa runs JavaScript inside WebAssembly (as the last resort only when we can’t run JavaScript in Dynamic Workers).
  • Linebender libraries provide text layout and 2D graphics, and Krilla generates PDF output.

These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices.

Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result.

All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together.

Run your own Kitesurf

To run Kitesurf locally, follow the repository's build requirements, then clone the repository, install dependencies, and start the engine:

      
git clone https://github.com/cloudflare/kitesurf.git
cd kitesurf
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm run dev

The first build compiles the Rust core and its dependencies, so give it some time. Subsequent builds reuse the build cache. Finally wrangler starts a local development server at http://127.0.0.1:8787. Open that address to try a page in Chrome DevTools, or use it programmatically.

You can use puppeteer with a NodeJS script:

      
import puppeteer from "puppeteer-core";

const browser = await puppeteer.connect({
  browserWSEndpoint: "ws://127.0.0.1:8787/devtools/browser",
});

try {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto("https://example.com/");
  await page.screenshot({ path: "page.png" });
} finally {
  await browser.disconnect();
}

Or you can point your AI harness at the local CDP port (agents love CDP) and watch it take full control of Kitesurf.

Deploy to your Cloudflare account

When you’re done changing and testing locally, you can deploy the engine to your own account and use Kitesurf from there instead of the Browser Run managed APIs we provide. Note that a Workers Paid plan is required because Kitesurf uses Dynamic Workers to create isolated Workers for pages.

From the repository root:

      
pnpm run deploy

Help us make it better

As with all of our open-sourced projects, Kitesurf lives in Github and we welcome forks and contributions. However, note that Kitesurf is under heavy development and we are focusing on making the engine more compatible (check out Web Platform Test evolution), more reliable, and efficient.

Start with the contribution guidelines if you want to contribute. Open an issue with a minimal reproduction or a proposed approach, and get vouched by a maintainer before opening a pull request. Focused fixes with tests, clear evidence, and a well-defined scope are much easier to review than large rewrites or unrelated cleanup, but all contribution does not have to be code: a small page that reproduces a rendering bug, a failing automation workflow, or a clear documentation correction can help us move forward.

Stay tuned

Kitesurf is evolving quickly. Stay tuned for updates in the blog and our changelog, and keep an eye on the official landing page for the latest on standards compatibility in Web Platform Tests page and benchmarks.

And come chat with the team on Discord. We’re building a browser for agents, and we’d love your help making it better.

entries.title: Adapting to AI penetration testing orchestrators: The Modern Security Model
entries.summary: AI-orchestrated penetration testing platforms like ARTEX have become increasingly powerful tools enabling effective attacks on exposed infrastructure. Here we share Cloudflare’s observations and recommended countermeasures.
entries.content:
Over the last month, the number of Large Language Model (LLM) penetration testing and orchestration frameworks has exploded. Just a few weeks ago, ARTEX — an open source agentic penetration testing system that automates offensive security workflows — was the only framework available. In just the last three days, we have seen over 50 framework families attempt to scan Cloudflare customers globally. The number of Internet Protocol (IP) addresses seen running these frameworks has grown into the thousands and continues to increase daily. The proliferation of these frameworks has significantly changed the status quo in cyber defense: defenders are struggling to keep up with the volumetric nature of these autonomously guided attacks.

ARTEX was taken down by its creator Autumn-27 on October 8. (“The malicious exploitation of this tool runs entirely counter to its original intent,” they wrote in Chinese.) But in the month since, the ecosystem has exploded with new fragmented versions of it. There are now over 12,000 repositories, with several hundred unique forks containing lineage from the original repository. Additionally, hundreds of other similar agentic orchestration frameworks have been created since October 8. Daily requests of AI penetration testing (pentesting) and exploitation tools has grown by 30x since October 1. These tools have also begun chaining stolen customer credentials in some of the more complex attacks, such as lateral movement chaining throughout an environment.

We expect these frameworks to continue to proliferate, and every organization should be prepared to address this threat. To counter LLM-based pentest frameworks, we recommend that all organizations adopt what we call the Modern Security Model, which has six key pillars:

  • Fortify the front gate: Implement a Web Application Firewall (WAF) with advanced rules such as rate limits.
  • Security station in the foyer: Anomaly detection on all web applications your customers access.
  • Identify phony visitors: Implement Bot Defense.
  • Remove the back door: Implement Identity-Gated Access for all high-risk external and internal web applications.
  • Inspect deliveries: Enforce validated schemas and explicit security controls.
  • Neighborhood watch: Implement Threat Intelligence to gain visibility into attacks.

What is an LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrator?

Open-source pentesting frameworks are able to orchestrate AI agents to carry out stages of the traditional Cyber Kill Chain at scale. Tools like ARTEX have the ability to quickly plug in existing Model Context Protocol (MCP) and connect traditional standalone pentesting tools in novel ways. Some even allow operator direction on what type of task to accomplish. These tools can map and enumerate environments, both from the inside and outside. ARTEX and its forks map assets and environments onto a graph, allowing multiple independent parallel agents to enumerate, verify, prototype, and attack at the speed of inference. These tools turn compromises into a hill-climbable problem, which agents are specifically good at.

The AI LLM pentesting tools that currently exist

We are currently tracking 50+ AI LLM agents. The table below shows the top five LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrators. Each is extremely popular (1k+ GitHub stars) and fully autonomous. The fully autonomous nature of these agents represents a doctrinal shift in offensive cyber capabilities:

  • Human skills are no longer the limit: A harness performs every step of the OODA loop by observing the environment, orienting itself to prioritize valuable and/or vulnerable targets, decide on an action, and act autonomously.
  • Speed increase: Having multiple parallel agents working towards a goal is a large shift compared to single operator or multiple operator augmented by AI.
  • Scale: A single operator can target multiple organizations at the same time, greatly increasing their blast radius.
  • Small mistakes are easily discovered: Autonomous frameworks relentlessly and systematically test exposed services, including their configurations.

Architecture

Planning model

Built-in capabilities/execution environment

Post-exploitation capabilities

ARTEX (and forks)

Planner and parallel agents

Graph of goals, leads, and findings is linked to separate asset graph of target

Directly on host or container with network/root access, can install/develop tools as needed

Nothing built-in, requires user instruction

LuaN1aoAgent

Supervisor agent, planner agent, and generic executor agents

Three graphs, with goals/tasks/blockers, evidence/hypothesises/exploits, and target/local

Container with network/user access, can develop tools as needed and install user packages

Built-in SSH and Chisel for tunneling and attempted reconnection after disruption

Decepticon

Orchestrator agent dispatching specialist sub-agents

Graph of objectives with prerequisites

Kali container running as root, can develop tools as needed

Dedicated post-access, Active Directory and cloud pivoting skills

Cairn

Dispatcher orchestrating work to existing AI harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, Pi)

Graph of facts and leads; new nodes trigger dispatcher

Kali container with root access or directly on host, can develop tools as needed

Prompt guidance and Kali tools

PentestGPT-Agent

Supervisor agent and one generic executor agent

Task list with dependencies, goals, and evidence

Run on host, can develop tools as needed

Nothing built-in, requires user instruction

Observations from the world's largest network

As of November 12, ARTEX and its forks make up over 60% of currently known AI penetration testing orchestrators. The charts below help us understand how adoption of these tools has changed over the past six weeks. Since the removal of the original ARTEX repository on October 8, traffic has grown more than tenfold, and has increased more than 30x since October 1.

As demonstrated above, the takedown of ARTEX on October 8 (and widespread reporting of it) likely caused a hydra effect, where the removal of the original repository led to a massive increase in the number of forks and modifications which can be seen in the steep acceleration of unique instances around October 8.

Identity-chained LLM exploitation

Over the last eight weeks, our Cloudforce One team has been called into multiple incident response investigations involving ARTEX and ARTEX-derived LLM exploitation frameworks. We’ve seen firsthand how exposed credentials are being chained with LLM-based exploitation frameworks to gain the upper hand over defenders.

We observed multiple incidents in which a threat actor gained initial access to a hyperscaler environment and pivoted directly into the customer's Cloudflare environment. Root-cause analysis revealed a common credential hygiene failure. Attackers repeatedly compromised static, non-expiring tokens running inside CI/CD pipelines, which granted broad, cross-environment access across the organization's hyperscaler infrastructure. LLM frameworks greatly expand the likelihood of a client’s API key being laterally leveraged to take over other tenant environments.

ARTEX in action

As part of one incident response investigation, our team observed ARTEX gaining access to a compromised account-level API token previously used for CI/CD with no IP restrictions or rate limiting. Available evidence indicated that the compromise most likely originated through a third-party hyperscaler.

We observed that a large number of new Worker scripts had been created with distinct names such as artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-*, and artex-do-*. The naming of each Worker script correlated to distinct behaviors and actions it was taking, and was often postfixed by an alphanumeric identifier. We observed activity in excess of 69 requests per minute across multiple unique parts of their Cloudflare infrastructure and 400 database dump requests in an hour. We also observed attempted persistence mechanisms and attempts to validate session tokens for other third-party applications. While we believe that much of this activity was lightly guided by the human operator, this is just one example of the speed and breadth that ARTEX and similar frameworks can achieve post-compromise.

Our recommendation: the Modern Security Model

Large Language Models increase the ability of a threat actor to rapidly iterate through the Cyber Kill Chain against a target. They do this by giving the actor the advantage of speed and validation. Each step of the Cyber Kill Chain can be validated and fed into the next stage of the attack. This level of orchestration is unparalleled and effectively vaporizes legacy cyber security models. A modern model must be used against these attacks.

To help explain this model further, let’s use the metaphor of protecting a house on an estate. Each section below outlines how to defend against the threat at each step.

Fortify the front gate: implement traffic control and a WAF with advanced rules

Before anyone even sets foot on your lawn, they have to reach the perimeter fence.

On an unprotected estate, an adversary can drive an endless fleet of decoy trucks straight into your driveway, completely blocking the entrance and smashing through the barriers (Layer 3/4 volumetric floods and direct IP probing).

With perimeter gate security in place, all incoming traffic is routed through massive, distributed outer gates miles away from the main house. Rogue delivery trucks are filtered out to the highway, rogue utility tunnels trying to wiretap your property are severed, and only legitimate foot traffic ever reaches your home address.

Network traffic control serves as an important role in stopping volumetric attacks.

A security station in the foyer: anomaly detection

Once visitors arrive at the main entry, they meet a strict security station at the foyer.

Automated prowlers don't just kick the door; they disguise themselves. They attempt weird ways to get in the door — stuffing paper into the lock, trying variations like 

//front-door//back-room/
 to trick the mechanism into swinging open.

The security guard at the door enforces clear rules:

  • You cannot knock 500 times in five seconds.
  • You cannot disguise your path with trickery.
  • You cannot attempt to roll a massive flatbed cart through the front hall to haul away the house's internal blueprints (diagnostic heap dumps). Suspicious behavior is turned away immediately.
  • Implement security keys and hardware based FIDO keys.

Web Application Firewall (WAF) serves as a key defense mechanism in stopping application exploitation through rate limits and anomaly detection.

Identify phony visitors: implement Bot Defense

A sophisticated intruder rarely looks like a masked burglar; they disguise themselves as ordinary visitors. But automated agents, headless browser scrapers, and AI reconnaissance tools don't act like real people.

They don't blink, their posture is unnervingly rigid, their cadence is mechanical, and their "identification" is often a sloppy imitation of a real visitor badge.

Bot Defense and challenges act as behavioral specialists watching the crowd through one-way glass. It flags the unnatural cadence, catches the synthetic micro-behaviors, and quietly escorts the machines off the property before they can touch a single doorknob.

Remove the back door: implement Identity-Gated Access and micro-segmentation

Many homes historically were built with side doors or a cellar hatch (internal admin panels, 

/actuator
 diagnostic endpoints, and remote gateways). Even if locked, a prowler could stand on the sidewalk, shine a flashlight on the cellar door, and start picking the lock.

Zero Trust application access does something radical: it bricks up the doorway from the outside and restricts which rooms can be entered.

To anyone wandering the perimeter, the cellar door does not exist. There is no lock to pick, no handle to rattle, and no light on inside. The only way in is with an escort who checks your biometric badge, confirms your device has a clean bill of health, and steps you directly into the specific room you need — leaving the rest of the house out of view.

For those who do enter, you have to ensure they cannot breach rooms next to the room they enter. Micro-segmentation is a highly effective strategy at stopping lateral movement. It limits compromised credentials from breaching production, test, and development systems.

Inspect deliveries: enforce validated schemas and explicit security controls

You receive daily supply deliveries to your estate — groceries, mail, maintenance parts. In digital terms, this is your incoming API traffic, which must be inspected and verified.

Intruders often attempt to bypass controls by sending unvalidated payloads or forged delivery manifests meant for restricted internal systems.

The porch protocol mandates thorough inspection and schema validation for all traffic:

  • Every incoming request must undergo OpenAPI schema validation to ensure it strictly conforms to expected definitions and structures.
  • Drivers and couriers must present validated mutual TLS (mTLS) certificates to establish trusted, authenticated connections.
  • Any request failing inspection or missing valid credentials is rejected immediately at the boundary.
  • Default-Deny Posture: Every positive security implementation ends with an explicit deny-all rule at the bottom of the ruleset.

Neighborhood watch: implement threat intelligence to gain visibility into attacks

Even with ironclad walls, an isolated property can be vulnerable if a syndicate invents a brand-new infiltration technique across town.

Threat intelligence acts as your warning network with neighboring estates. When a rogue actor sets up a new command-and-control safehouse down the road or begins deploying dynamic tunneling vans in your district, you receive an early dossier. Your estate updates its watchlists, recalibrates its sensors, and slams the gate shut before the actor ever turns onto your street.

How to get real-time help

ARTEX and similar LLM-based frameworks pose a significant challenge to legacy cyber defense models. Even the historical defense-in-depth model — which emphasizes a classic network DMZ — falls short in today's complex architectures. Tomorrow's attacks will only advance as orchestration tools become the new normal.

Securing legacy equipment and on-premises devices requires an identity-gated approach that logically makes these devices impossible to reach on the Internet. Beyond identity, slowing or making lateral movement more noisy is the goal of micro-segmentation. This architecture emphasizes a containment-first approach to security, which is essential when users are consistently losing their keys. When combined, the elements of the Modern Security Model are the answer to this vexing problem.

If you are facing an active security incident and need the Cloudforce One team on the ground to help respond to the incident or require threat intelligence support, please contact us immediately. If you need help implementing the Modern Security Model outlined here, please contact our Solutions Engineering team.

entries.title: Introducing Spend Management: Spending limits and alerts for Cloudflare
entries.summary: Spend Management adds opt-in spending caps for Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects, and more products soon. Here is how we built the metering pipeline that turns usage into runtime decisions.
entries.content:
Spend controls have been at the top of the list of most requested features from developers building on our developer platform for quite some time now. With more than 10 million developers now building on Cloudflare, this matters more than ever.

Although we’ve had usage notifications and budget alerts available to paid plans for a while, this doesn’t solve the problem completely; informing is not the same as controlling.

You can now set spending thresholds and choose to have Cloudflare pause activity when those limits are reached, thus avoiding unexpected bills from unplanned usage. Today, we're introducing Spend Management in Beta, for any pay-as-you-go (PayGo) customer, starting with Workers and Durable Objects.

Use Spend Management alongside AI Gateway spend limits to manage compute and AI inference costs across your application. AI Gateway already supports per-user and per-model budgets for Workers AI and other AI providers, applied to requests routed through your gateway.

How it works

You can start using Spend Management using the dashboard, cf CLI, or REST API.

In the dashboard, head over to Manage Account > Billing > Spend limits and enable the products for which you want to control spending.

When you enable controls on a product, you can define a spending limit, specify a recipient email for notifications, and set one or more alert thresholds.

If you configure a recipient email, Cloudflare will send notifications when the evaluated spend reaches one of the thresholds or your spending limit. When the limit is reached, a blocking policy is enforced and your product is paused automatically.

If you go to the dashboard, you can see the current billing cycle costs for each supported product in near real time (under 10 minutes), and manage your settings and thresholds from there. The overview panel tells you which products have thresholds and limits configured. In this example, you can see that Workers triggered two alerts before hitting the hard limit.

Note that the billing cycle starts when the paid subscription begins, not when you deploy a Worker or create a spending cap; a subscription starting October 10 generally has a cycle of October 10-November 10 — not a calendar month.

The dashboard also shows an audit log, so you can see who changed a limit and when, or when a cap was reached.

As with most Cloudflare services, Spend Management is also an API that you can use programmatically; the documentation can be found in our Developer Documentation. Here’s an example, but using the API:

      
curl --fail-with-body --request POST \
  "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/${CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID}/billing/spend-policies" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "name": "Workers spending cap",
    "product_id": "workers",
    "enabled": true,
    "threshold_cents": 10000,
    "action": "usage_block",
    "notification_email": "me@example.com"
  }'

And, of course, you can use cf, the CLI for the entire Cloudflare API:

      
cf billing spend-policies list
cf billing spend-policies create
cf billing spend-policies get
cf billing spend-policies update
cf billing spend-policies delete
cf billing spend-policies audit list
cf billing spend-policies activity list

cf billing spend-policies create --body '{
  "name": "Workers spending cap",
  "product_id": "workers",
  "enabled": true,
  "threshold_cents": 10000,
  "action": "usage_block",
  "notification_email": "me@example.com"
}'

Once a cap is enforced, new invocations of that product are rejected. Note that we only pause customer-code invocations that incur costs — in Workers, for example, Cron Triggers and Queue consumer invocations are paused, but static assets continue to be served.

To resume service, you can:

  • Raise the limit above the current cycle’s accumulated spend.
  • Disable or delete the blocking policy.
  • Wait until the next billing cycle, when the existing block expires.

That’s it. You can start using Spend Management for Workers and Durable Objects today, and other products will follow soon.

Read on to learn how we built the system, and what’s going to happen next.

How we built Spend Management

As easy and straightforward as it seems on the surface, building a system like this at Cloudflare scale was no small feat. From an invocation anywhere on our distributed network to a blocking decision that we need to apply globally, building Spend Management required working with multiple teams, changing code in existing systems, and creating new systems from scratch.

Let’s start by looking at the bird's-eye view of a capped billable event:

Now let's dig deeper.

Collecting and aggregating close to the source

Each invocation produces usage measurements: requests, CPU time, execution duration, or storage operations, depending on the product. But transporting and processing this volume of raw data all the way from the sources down to the rating engine would not scale or be efficient.

So what we do is we collect and aggregate the measurements as close to the source as possible using a two-stage metering pipeline that combines events into usage aggregates, so the engine sees accumulated usage rather than having to process all the events one by one.

Let's look at a diagram.

The first stage reduces raw-event volume close to parsing down to one-minute windows. Each metering parser converts raw events into usage measurements, then combines matching measurements into typically one-minute buckets. Still, several records can describe the same account and time window.

In the second stage, a separate service merges those first-stage partial aggregates using the same grouping rules, but over typically five-minute windows, and further reduces the volume before downstream processing by the Usage Engine. Here we also archive the consolidated aggregates; this gives us a durable dataset for later analytics and reconciliation.

The nice thing about this two-stage pipeline is that it reduces the raw event volume early, so the downstream engines process only the aggregated usage they need to calculate spend and act on it. That’s what makes this practical at Cloudflare’s scale.

Usage Engine: account-partitioned processing

The Usage Engine translates aggregated measurements into usage records, which are standardized records containing the account, usage window, metric, quantity, and relevant dimensions. In other words, it maps product-specific meters into supported usage metrics.

We partition processing by account, so an account’s usage and subscription information meet in the same place. That lets us maintain its accumulated usage and apply included allowances without coordinating across pricing processors on every update.

As you can see, we run different partitions in parallel, giving us a way to spread the work across accounts while keeping each account’s pricing state together. Also note that each partition keeps both a local state for fast access, and also a durable write-ahead logging (WAL) changelog on disk. This buys us:

  • Less cross-partition coordination: each account’s usage and subscription state stay together.
  • Consistent pricing: usage updates share the same allowance and accumulated-spend state.
  • Parallel processing: different partitions calculate spend independently.
  • Recoverability: durable state lets replacement processors rebuild and resume after failures, if necessary.

Then, finally, the usage metrics are fed into the Rating Engine.

The Rating Engine

The Rating Engine is the most important block of Spend Management; it turns usage into monetary value and it’s what’s able to answer the question: “Given what this account has consumed, its subscription, and its pricing, how much has it spent so far?”

Here’s how it works.

In essence, the Rating Engine brings together three things:

  • Usage records: quantities such as requests and CPU milliseconds.
  • Subscription information: the account’s billing period and plan changes.
  • Pricing rules: rates, included allowances, and billing rounding.

Usage data and subscriptions are independent streams

Usage and subscription updates arrive as independent streams, so we can’t assume they reach the Rating Engine in order. Furthermore, we have to be able to recover from a data processing failure or missing subscription information from, say, a failed webhook.

If usage arrives before the subscription information needed to price it, we retain it as pending and revisit it when that information becomes available. This lets us tolerate temporary delays without treating unpriced usage as free.

Tracking accumulated spend

Finally, we calculate and track accumulated spend. The Rating Engine uses a product catalog database that defines usage metrics, including allowances, rates, and rounding rules, alongside the account’s subscription information. One million CPU milliseconds doesn’t necessarily mean an extra charge: the engine first applies the account’s included CPU allowance, then prices any excess. It prices accumulated usage rather than rounding and charging for each request independently.

Once the accumulated spend is calculated, two steps follow:

  • Policy evaluation: decide whether one or more warning or blocking thresholds have been reached.
  • Reporting: we show estimated usage charges in the dashboard via our APIs, and we send out email alerts (via Cloudflare Email Service) if necessary.

Asynchronous cap enforcement

The Rating Engine doesn’t sit in the request path or directly reject requests. Instead, the policy service sends the cap to our runtime configuration service and Quicksilver, our internal key-value store developed to enable fast global replication and low-latency access at planet scale. This propagates it to all our nodes asynchronously.

Once the cap reaches Quicksilver, the runtime picks it up during its periodic refresh and starts rejecting capped invocations or operations.

In other words, enforcement uses local state, so requests never have to wait on the Rating Engine. By reusing our existing runtime account-limit architecture, we keep rating out of the request path while distributing caps across the global network.

What’s next

Any pay-as-you-go customer can start using Spend Management today. While this is a major milestone in our roadmap, it’s also just the start. Let us share some of our plans for the next few weeks and months ahead.

More products

We are starting with caps for Workers and Durable Objects, but you’ll be able to measure and cap many other Cloudflare products and primitives in the near future. We’ve built the system in a way that makes it easy and familiar for our products to onboard, so expect the catalog to grow.

Closer to real time

While near real time under 10 minutes is a great benchmark, we’re not satisfied with it, and being the stubborn engineers we are, we have pretty good ideas on how to reduce that time even further. Expect us to shorten the gap between measurement and enforcement over time, hopefully to under a minute.

Agent and application-based budgets

Right now, we measure spend by products and primitives, but there are other useful dimensions to explore when controlling costs. For example, a developer might want to monitor the costs of a specific application — such as a Worker script that uses other primitives like R2 or Workers AI. How can we measure the aggregated cost of an entire application and pause that application, rather than disabling the underlying primitives across all customer applications?

Another compelling use case for cost controls is AI agents. We’ve all read horror stories about rogue agents entering unconstrained recursive reasoning loops to brute-force a problem — generating thousands of dollars in costs from high-frequency, expensive API calls, not to mention causing denial-of-service (DoS) issues on databases and other services. AI Gateway already lets you give an agent a budget for AI requests routed through it. A task can also consume compute, database, and storage resources. We want to make it possible to budget for that broader resource use across products.

You’ll be able to tag the calls from your agents and our pipeline will carry that metadata from the runtime through to the Rating Engine. That will let us attribute spend and pause an application or an agentic task across products, without interrupting other unrelated applications.

Get started

This launch is a first step toward making spend controls a normal part of building on Cloudflare, alongside deploying code and monitoring your applications.

Check out the billing developer documentation for more information. Start using Spend Management and tell us what works, what’s missing, or where more granular budgets would help.

Join us on Discord or our socials. We’re listening!

entries.title: Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm
entries.summary: Cloudflare is building an experimental consensus service using a never-before-deployed consensus algorithm, QuePaxa. In this post we explain how QuePaxa works and why we chose it.
entries.content:
Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat, an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023).

QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well.

Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat.

Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works.

What we’re building and why it’s unique

Meerkat is a distributed system in which replicas agree upon an ordered log of events, where each event is decided by a consensus algorithm.

Consensus algorithms allow a group of machines to agree on a single shared truth, even if some of those machines crash or disconnect. Consensus algorithms provide an important guarantee: machines never decide conflicting values. This ensures Meerkat replicas’ logs never diverge.

Meerkat uses its consensus-powered log to expose applications like a key-value store, where each entry in the log is a 

get
 or a 
put
. Because the consensus algorithm guarantees replicas’ logs never diverge, they all construct the same key-value (KV) state. Comparable consensus-powered systems include Consul, etcd, and Apache ZooKeeper.

Unlike similar systems, however, Meerkat was designed for global scale. A Meerkat cluster may be distributed across continents and connected by links that often exhibit high and variable latency. This is an unusual setup for consensus systems, which are usually deployed in smaller, more local networks, and have strict latency requirements.

The challenges of consensus at a global scale

While all consensus algorithms ensure that replicas agree on the same value, many of them become disproportionately unavailable or slow when network conditions degrade (but machines do not crash). We have seen this happen firsthand: in 2020, the partial failure of a core Cloudflare network switch caused a consensus-powered system to degrade and the dashboard to operate 80x slower than usual, for six hours. Critically, the system lost no data. But it became unavailable for writes until the issue was resolved, which is unacceptable.

Ideally, a consensus algorithm should be able to make progress despite latency spikes and broken connections, not just replica failures. This is particularly a problem at global scale, where faults are more likely to originate in the network, and not our own servers.

Let’s examine two common traits of consensus algorithms that can lead to degradation under hostile network conditions: destructive interference and fault detection. Later, we’ll see how QuePaxa sidesteps both of these issues.

Destructive interference and leaders

Consider Paxos, the veritable grandfather of most consensus algorithms. A lot of consensus algorithms inherit the structure of Paxos – both the good and the not-so-good bits.

Leaving an egregious amount of detail out, here’s how Paxos works. There are two kinds of processes: proposers and acceptors. Abstractly, the goal of the system is for a majority of acceptors to agree on a value proposed by some proposer. There are two phases: the 

Prepare
 phase, and the 
Accept
 phase. In the 
Prepare
 phase, any proposer can send a ballot number out to a majority of acceptors. This ballot number serves as a promise – acceptors will only accept proposals with that ballot number or higher. Then, in the 
Accept
 phase, the proposer sends its proposal along with the ballot number to a majority of acceptors again. If a majority of acceptors still hold the ballot number of the proposal, the majority accepts it, and the proposer can safely decide the proposal.

Challenges arise when two or more proposers submit proposals at the same time. Specifically, another proposer can interleave its own higher ballot number in between the two phases, blocking any lower ballots. Two proposers can repeatedly block each other from progressing – effectively competing for acceptance.

When proposers compete and block each other in this way, we say that they destructively interfere. Destructive interference gets worse as more proposers propose their own ballots. The more concurrent proposers there are, the more likely it is that the system gets stuck repeatedly proposing. Even if none of the replicas have crashed or are unavailable, multiple proposers and misbehaving networks can block Paxos. Formally, we say that Paxos does not guarantee liveness (i.e., that proposals are eventually decided) without assuming that, at some point, all messages arrive within a bounded amount of time — an assumption known as partial synchrony.

To avoid multiple proposers constantly competing, most deployed consensus algorithms, like Raft, Multi-Paxos, and Viewstamped Replication, add a special leader proposer. The leader is the only replica that can make proposals. Centralizing the proposing power in one replica forces an order on concurrent requests, avoids competing proposals, and has the added benefit of getting decisions done in an optimal single network round-trip, instead of two. While the leader is healthy and the network is well-behaved, leader-based protocols are fast.

The trade-off is that the leader must remain operational and reachable. When it fails, becomes too slow, or is disconnected from the cluster, the system stalls. The only solution is for the remaining replicas to detect that the leader has failed, and elect a new one in its place.

When leader recovery is unstable

When a leader fails, the system must recover by electing a new one. Interestingly, leader recovery is often how destructive interference sneaks right back into a leader-based system.

Consider Raft. For safety reasons, Raft elects a new leader using a majority vote. A replica that suspects that the leader has failed announces itself as a candidate for leadership and requests a vote from other replicas. If more than half of the replicas agree to vote for the candidate, it becomes the new leader. If they don’t, then a new election is called, and the candidates try again.

Multiple replicas can become candidates — all they need to do is detect that the leader is down. The candidates may then all try to acquire a majority vote simultaneously. The problem is that the candidates will compete for the majority vote, which means Raft’s elections suffer from the destructive interference we just saw in Paxos: two replicas can mutually prevent each other from getting support from a majority and becoming the leader. The more elections fail, the more replicas will try to get themselves elected leader.

Even if the leader stops being faulty, elections continue to disrupt what could have been normal system functioning. This is known as a metastable failure: a failure pattern that perpetuates itself even when the initial cause of failure is removed. A two-second network outage — or a momentarily faulty network switch — can make the leader appear to be faulty and force a leader election, which can fail, and force further elections. The outage will be over in two seconds, but the election can continue for much longer as candidates continue to block each other.

Ideally, consensus algorithms wouldn’t need any recovery process, as they are complicated, prone to interference, and introduce another source of downtime.

When fault detection goes awry

The problem of destructive interference in leader elections is compounded by trigger-happy fault-detection, especially in wide-area networks. In order for leader-based consensus algorithms to choose a new leader, replicas must first detect that the leader has failed. However, if replicas detect leader-failures inaccurately, the system may spend an inordinate amount of time in recovery, not handling requests.

In a distributed system, where machines are separated over a network, fault detection will ultimately depend on expectations. A process cannot directly observe that a remote process has failed; it can only observe that an expected message has or hasn’t arrived. We need a predictable pattern of communication, such as heartbeats or acknowledgements, to tell us that a machine is healthy. If an expected message does not arrive within the expected time, we suspect a fault. The difficulty lies in managing those expectations.

In real networks, especially wide-area networks, messages don’t always arrive when predicted. There is no guaranteed upper bound on the time that it takes for messages to arrive. That’s not to say that the network is slow, or that it is unreliable — most messages arrive within the time we expect them to. Instead, sudden bursts of latency and losses in connectivity can, momentarily, and without warning, increase the time it takes for any message to traverse the network. We call such networks asynchronous.

The big issue with asynchronous networks is that if some server doesn’t reply in a given amount of time, we don’t really know if the server has failed or if the network is just slow — the two are indistinguishable over the network. Any practical fault detector has to make a guess based on how long it has been waiting compared to its expectation, and sometimes that guess will be wrong.

In leader-based algorithms, that guess is exactly what triggers leader elections. Sometimes the leader is down; sometimes its messages are late, or the connection is silently broken. The protocol cannot know which one happened before it reacts. If the guess is wrong, and a replica thinks the leader is faulty when it actually isn’t, then an election begins and the entire system must stop. Until the leader is replaced, no progress is made — and as we just saw, that can take a while.

Fault detection is fundamentally error-prone in asynchronous networks, and when the detector makes a mistake, we get downtime.

When fault detection is slow

Even when a fault detector guesses correctly, there are issues. Fault detectors react to failures by observing messages on the network, and so their response time has to scale with network latency — the detector’s timeout can’t be below the network latency. This is why Raft is commonly deployed with an election timeout of five to ten times the network round-trip time. It has to be high enough to give a chance for the leader to signal that it is alive, and avoid falsely triggering elections. The election timeout can be much lower than that, but since leader elections completely stop the system, timeouts are usually set conservatively high.

Roughly speaking, a round trip halfway across the world is measured in hundreds of milliseconds. If an election timeout is several round trips, detecting a failed coordinator can take around a second. Even when fault detection is completely accurate, it is slow, and it is slowest in high-latency global networks. Until the detector reacts, the system is down.

Why QuePaxa is the right fit

We realized that any algorithm relying on a strict leader or accurate timeouts was inevitably going to stall in a consensus system that runs over the Internet. We searched for consensus algorithms designed for asynchronous environments — protocols that didn't rely on a well-behaved network or precise timing to function. This led us to QuePaxa, published in 2023 by Tennage & Băsescu et al.

The most notable thing about QuePaxa is how it can efficiently reach consensus in a single round trip under favorable network conditions, but also gracefully degrades performance during latency spikes, connectivity issues, and server failures. QuePaxa achieves this by solving the exact problems we just discussed through three key design choices: having an optional leader, completely removing the reliance on fault detection, and designing for constructive interference between proposers.

In QuePaxa, much like in Paxos, there are two roles: proposers and recorders. Proposers submit proposals to be decided on, and recorders serve as intermediaries between proposers, recording every proposal they see.

Instead of having proposers compete to get their own proposals decided, in QuePaxa, proposers will cooperatively work towards a proposal that everyone supports. QuePaxa does this by assigning a priority to proposals, in the form of a random number. The optional leader gets an exclusive maximum priority. During execution, proposers submit their proposals to the recorders, who propagate the proposal to other active proposers. When proposers receive a proposal from a recorder with a higher priority than theirs, they adopt the new proposal as their own, i.e., begin broadcasting the higher priority proposal instead. In general, proposers in QuePaxa work together to decide on the highest priority proposal that they collectively know. This means proposers can’t lock each other out of deciding on a proposal, indefinitely.

The caveat is that it might not be possible to spread proposals around well enough to agree on a proposal, and so proposers have to try again, with each attempt constituting a round. However, as more proposers submit proposals, the more likely they are to converge on the highest priority proposal. This is what makes QuePaxa a randomized algorithm: the randomly generated priorities of non-leader proposers are likely — but not guaranteed — to lead to consensus on the highest known priority, in a round. Yet, given enough rounds, it is guaranteed that proposers agree on a proposal.

One proposer is designated the leader. The leader is the only proposer capable of deciding in a single round trip. The leader always proposes with the highest priority; if the leader knows it spread its proposal before any other proposer, then it can decide immediately. Clients aren’t forced to make requests to the leader — any proposer can propose. If the leader goes down, then clients can keep making requests to other proposers. The leader is completely optional. The leader is simply more likely to decide, than any other proposer, and do so faster, in a single round trip.

However, because the leader is the only one that can decide in a single round trip, we want to use it whenever possible. To exploit this fast path without creating a single point of failure, clients sending proposals to the system hedge their bets: they send their requests for proposals to every replica, and the non-leader replicas will wait for a small timeout, so the leader can propose and decide on its own. In our own implementation of QuePaxa, we actually deviate from the paper and have clients wait the hedge timeout instead of the replicas, to reduce the amount of messages we send over the network, but the overall result is the same.

This hedging timeout is very different from the timeouts used in Raft or Multi-Paxos. It is not fault detection, and so isn’t constrained by network latency; it is locally determined by replicas and can be as small as they want it to be. In Raft, having a five-millisecond timeout in a network with 100-millisecond latency would completely freeze the system. But in QuePaxa, a five-millisecond hedge timeout only increases the number of active proposers.

However, hedging isn’t free: the more proposers there are, the more proposals get broadcast, and the more likely it is that replicas fail to decide in a round. Instead, hedging provides a tradeoff: we can react faster to leader changes by lowering the hedge timeout, but we incur extra bandwidth costs and may take more time to decide. That’s a tradeoff we're more than willing to make.

If the QuePaxa leader goes down, we can recover as fast as we want — we’re not bound by network latency. This is how QuePaxa gets around fault detection: since anyone can propose, not just the leader, QuePaxa can proactively deal with leader failures by hedging, rather than reacting to failures.

How QuePaxa works under the hood

To understand how QuePaxa gives us all of these nice properties, let’s look at how QuePaxa actually works.

QuePaxa works in rounds made up of four phases. If a proposal hasn’t been decided on in the last phase, a new round is started, and QuePaxa starts over. At the start of each phase, proposers broadcast their currently adopted proposal to all recorders. Once a proposer receives a reply from a majority of recorders, they advance to the next phase. Here’s the general outline of the phases:

  • Phase 0 (Propose and Adopt): Proposers randomly select a priority, send their proposals to recorders, and adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority of recorders. If it’s the first round and the leader knows its proposal reached a majority of recorders first, the leader decides immediately.
  • Phase 1 (Spread): Proposers spread their adopted proposal to a majority of recorders.
  • Phase 2 (Check and Decide): Proposers ask a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal seen in the previous phase. If it matches their own adopted proposal, they decide on it.
  • Phase 3 (Carry Forward): Any proposer that failed to decide prepares for the next round by adopting the best proposal they see from a majority of recorders.

Let’s walk through a couple of example executions and unpack how each phase contributes to the overall behavior we want out of QuePaxa. Each execution will have two proposers (one of which is the leader) and three recorders.

The Leader Fast Path (Phase 0): The first phase does three important things: it randomizes priorities (which it must do to circumvent the FLP impossibility theorem), checks if the leader reached a majority of support first, and helps proposers converge if the leader didn't. The leader’s proposal is not randomized, and will always have the highest possible priority.

In the example above, the leader's proposal reaches a majority of recorders before anyone else, and receives replies confirming it. The leader can safely decide right away. This might seem dangerous, but it is entirely safe thanks to a property called majority intersection: any two majorities of recorders always share at least one recorder. Because the leader reached a majority, any other proposer querying a majority will inevitably encounter the leader's proposal and adopt it. Since the leader’s proposal has the highest priority, any other proposer will adopt the leader’s proposal. It is impossible to decide on any other proposal.

Concurrent Slow Path (Phases 0-3): When there are concurrent proposers, however, it is not guaranteed that the leader will immediately decide. The leader might fail to reach a majority of recorders first, or it might receive a single reply supporting another proposer. Let's look at what happens when another proposer contests the leader.

Phase 0: Pictured below, a second proposer (shown in red) reaches the second and third recorders first. The fast path is blocked. Instead of competing, proposers adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority and move to the second phase. The two proposers could both converge to the leader’s proposal in this phase. For illustrative purposes, our example will prevent convergence by delaying the leader’s messages.

Phase 1: Proposers spread the proposal they just adopted in Phase 0 to a majority of recorders. The recorders keep track of the highest-priority proposal they observe. It is a simple but critical step: it prevents the protocol from later deciding on a lower-priority proposal. This is once again thanks to majority intersection: any majority queried in the following phase must include at least one recorder that saw the adopted proposal, in this phase. For illustrative purposes, we prevent convergence in this phase by delaying the leader’s message to the third recorder, so the recorder does not adopt the leader’s proposal.

Phase 2: Now, a decision can happen. Each proposer determines if a higher-priority proposal gained enough support to overtake its own by asking a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal observed during Phase 1. If the highest proposal returned is still their adopted proposal, they decide. In our diagram, the leader sees its own proposal returned by a majority and safely decides. The other proposer receives conflicting summaries, so it cannot decide yet. Like in Phase 1, recorders keep track of the highest priority proposal they received.

Phase 3: If a proposer doesn’t decide in Phase 2, it moves to the final cleanup phase to prepare for the next round. Proposers spread their proposals again and adopt the best they find among a majority of recorders. Here, the remaining proposer discovers the decided proposal and adopts it, heading into the next round.

This is deliberate — if there was some decision in the previous phase, then a majority of the recorders will have that proposal, and any remaining proposers are guaranteed to adopt it. We see here another instance of cooperation between proposers — even when a round fails, proposers try to converge on the same proposal heading into the next round.

Moving to the next round: After the fourth phase, proposers move on to the next round. At this point, there is no more leader fast path, and the only way to decide is by converging in the third phase. Importantly, due to proposal adoption, it becomes exponentially easier to decide as rounds progress. The QuePaxa paper predicts that each round has a 50% chance of deciding, but in practice, that probability is much higher, thanks to convergence.

Putting all four phases together, we can see where QuePaxa gets its resilience. The first phase gives the leader its one-round-trip fast path. If that fast path fails, random priorities and proposal adoption help proposers converge instead of compete. The second and third phases make it safe to decide, thanks to majority intersection, while the fourth carries what proposers learned into the next round, in case proposers don’t decide.

No proposer has to detect that the leader has failed before making progress, and a failed round doesn’t throw away the work already done. When the network behaves, QuePaxa is fast. When it doesn’t, QuePaxa keeps moving.

How QuePaxa makes Meerkat possible

In our own evaluations of Meerkat, where we had servers spanning nearly all continents, we’ve directly experienced the impact that QuePaxa has on the overall performance and availability of the system. Meerkat continuously processes requests, even when the leader crashes, disconnects, or just becomes slow. At no point have we ever seen it completely stall. This is exactly what we wanted.

The rate at which Meerkat handles requests has also been generally predictable. Most decisions — upwards of 95% — are made by the leader in the first phase, which keeps our throughput fairly stable. In the instances where a decision isn't reached in the first phase, the throughput drops momentarily, down to at most a third of the usual rate, signaling that three round trips — so three phases — were needed to decide instead of just one. The system slows down, but does not grind to a halt.

QuePaxa also allows us to confidently switch out which replica acts as leader while the cluster is running. Since the leader isn’t the exclusive driver behind decisions and proposers are cooperative, a temporarily non-optimal leader isn’t as limiting as in other algorithms, where a leader misconfiguration could stall the system completely. We can dynamically tune which proposer is the leader without worrying too much about impacting the stability of a Meerkat cluster.

What we’ll be showing next

Designing Meerkat for a global network forced us to re-evaluate how we approach distributed consensus. Instead of sticking to familiar defaults that didn't quite fit our constraints, we looked to the decades of research produced by academia and industry. That search led us to QuePaxa.

Choosing QuePaxa meant choosing a less-traveled path. It has not been battle-tested as extensively as Raft or Paxos, and we’re also extending the original crash-stop design to support crash recovery. This demands careful engineering and stronger evidence of correctness than usual systems.

That is why we are formally verifying our QuePaxa implementation and Meerkat as a whole, alongside extensive simulation and fault-injection testing. Future posts in this series will explain how we verify Meerkat and QuePaxa’s Rust implementation, how we test failures that are difficult to reproduce in production, benchmarks, and what we have learned while turning an academic protocol into a production system.

Stay on the lookout for further Meerkat updates on the Cloudflare Blog, and if you want to learn more about research at Cloudflare, have a look at our work at Cloudflare Research.

entries.title: Launching the Vite Ecosystem Fund
entries.summary: Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to open source projects and maintainers. The recipients were chosen by a panel of Vite stack core team members, including maintainers not employed by Cloudflare.
entries.content:
Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to 44 projects and maintainers across the Vite ecosystem.

When VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we committed $1 million to strengthen the open source ecosystem around Vite. This round is just the start.

Sponsoring open source has always mattered, but now AI has made funding urgent.

AI is changing open source

AI has made open source more valuable while triggering more maintainer burnout. Previously, contributing to a project through either an issue or pull request meant you cared about it. In return, maintainers would review and provide feedback. AI changed the social contract of open source. Anyone can now create and submit AI-authored pull requests.

The most visible result is the influx of pull requests. As the number of PRs has gone up, the number of maintainers reviewing them has stayed constant. So each maintainer’s workload has grown.

During reviews, maintainers often find themselves speaking with an agent and not a person like they used to. If that’s the case, then why not cut out the middleman? Maintainers now have their own agents they can prompt to produce better results since they have more knowledge of the codebase.

AI has raised the pressure to produce. It’s made it easier for maintainers to ship features, performance improvements, and bug fixes that would not have been done otherwise. But it’s also made it easy for other projects to do the same. When another project adds overlapping features using AI, maintainers feel a need to keep up using AI. It can become a grinding cycle, where each project pushes the other to move faster. Along the way, some projects have grown in scope and lost sight of their original goals.

Maintainer burnout and sustainability have always been a problem — and now AI has accelerated those issues. That’s why sponsoring open source projects and supporting maintainers is so important in this moment.

One of the Vite Ecosystem Fund’s first recipients is e18e, a community focused on improving performance across the JavaScript ecosystem. Its lead, James Garbutt, has a long history in open source, and his work at e18e has helped make popular tools like Svelte, Storybook, and Nx faster. "Sponsorships make a huge difference and allow maintainers to dedicate more of their time to the things we all rely on," Garbutt says.

Fund distribution

The recipients of the Vite Ecosystem Fund were selected by a panel of core team members from Vite stack projects (Vite, Vitest, Rolldown, Oxc, Vite+), including maintainers not employed by Cloudflare.

The funding is allocated through Cloudflare's Open Collective as a combination of:

  • Contributions to ecosystem recipients
  • Stipends to core maintainers

We’re proud that Cloudflare has committed to making the open source ecosystem we rely on stronger and more sustainable. No project thrives in isolation.

We'll continue to distribute and draw down the committed amount every quarter.

Contributions to ecosystem recipients

This first round of sponsorships prioritized dependencies, ecosystem critical plugins, significant contributors, and projects that moved the ecosystem forward.

Stipends to core maintainers

The core maintainers of the Vite stack are eligible for a stipend of up to $4,000 per calendar month. Each maintainer can invoice at a rate of $50 per hour contributed that month.

Any time spent improving or supporting the project in some way counts towards this stipend: writing code, writing documentation, triaging issues, offering support in our Discord servers, attending meetings or meetups, contributing to our upstream dependencies, and so on.

Maintainers who are already being paid for or employed for this work do not receive stipends — for example, VoidZero employees are ineligible.

Cloudflare supports open source

Cloudflare’s mission is to help build a better Internet. Supporting open source falls squarely within that mission. The Vite Ecosystem Fund is only part of it.

Cloudflare committed an additional $1 million to sponsor open source projects in our Community Engineers Fund. We also provide Cloudflare credits to open source projects via Project Alexandria.

The Vite ecosystem has come this far because of all the maintainers and contributors who came together to build a community. These sponsorships are a small thank-you for all this hard work.
